title: Premature Speech EOS is Not a Dominant Failure Mode in Qwen2.5-Omni: An Empirical Study of Text-Length-Coupled Audio Stopping

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to test whether coupling speech stopping to generated text length improves speech-text consistency in an end-to-end omni-modal LLM. None of the prior papers explicitly address this purpose. While papers like [3] ("Soundwave") and [7] ("ELLA-V") discuss speech-text alignment issues, they focus on training strategies or architectural improvements rather than decode-time interventions for coupling speech stopping to text length. Papers such as [2] and [4] discuss joint speech-text decoding or multimodal generation but do not target the specific problem of improving speech-text consistency via length coupling.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, TLC-AS, is a training-free decode-time intervention that computes a minimum audio token floor from text word count and a calibrated words-per-second rate, masking the speech EOS token until the floor is reached. Paper [8] ("TED-TTS") introduces a training-free framework for intra-utterance emotion and duration control in TTS, which involves duration masking, but it does not compute a token floor based on text length or use a calibrated rate. Paper [22] ("DurIAN-E 2") uses duration-informed attention for expressive TTS synthesis, but this is a training-based mechanism and does not involve decode-time interventions. No prior paper describes a substantively equivalent mechanism.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses VoiceBench CommonEval (200 samples) to compare WER with and without the intervention. Paper [3] ("Soundwave") evaluates speech-text alignment using WER, and paper [7] ("ELLA-V") uses alignment-guided metrics for speech-text consistency. Both employ standard evaluation designs (WER-based comparison) for speech-text alignment, which matches the evaluation design here. The specific benchmark (VoiceBench CommonEval) is new, but the evaluation design itself is covered.

### Domain
The domain is omni-modal LLM speech generation. Papers [4] ("AudioGen-Omni") and [14] ("LTX-2") work in multimodal audio generation, including speech, and paper [7] ("ELLA-V") addresses speech generation in neural codec language modeling. These papers operate in the same general application area of multimodal or omni-modal speech generation, even though the specific sub-problem differs.

### Purpose
The contribution aims to establish whether premature EOS (end-of-sequence) emission is a dominant failure mode in Qwen2.5-Omni. None of the prior papers explicitly investigate premature EOS emission as a failure mode in Qwen2.5-Omni or any other omni-modal LLM. While some papers (e.g., [15]) discuss Qwen2.5-Omni's technical capabilities, they do not address this specific failure mode. Papers like [14], [23], [25], and [27] mention premature termination in unrelated contexts (e.g., PCR, beta-globin mRNA, or PTEN isoforms), but these are entirely distinct domains and mechanisms, and do not establish the same empirical relationship.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves measuring early-stopping frequency under a raised audio token cap and assessing WER (word error rate) change under TLC-AS. None of the prior papers describe a substantively equivalent mechanism for measuring early-stopping frequency or WER change under similar conditions. Papers like [6], [18], and [9] discuss WER in ASR systems, but they do not use the same measurement setup (raised token cap or TLC-AS). Similarly, [15] describes Qwen2.5-Omni's streaming capabilities but does not measure early-stopping frequency or WER changes under these specific conditions.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves measuring early-stopping frequency and WER change under specific conditions (raised audio token cap and TLC-AS). Papers like [6], [18], and [9] use WER as a metric in ASR systems, but they do not employ the same evaluation design (raised token cap or TLC-AS). No prior paper uses this specific evaluation setup, making the evaluation design genuinely new.

### Domain
The domain is omni-modal LLM speech generation. Papers [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [7], [15], and [16] all address omni-modal LLMs or speech generation, making the domain covered. While the specific sub-problem (premature EOS emission in Qwen2.5-Omni) is new, the general application area of omni-modal LLM speech generation is well-established in prior work.
